questions.stem: In which situation is the accommodating style the most appropriate choice for the nurse?
options: A coworker who must take a call about her sick child asks to swap break times, and the nurse has no preference.
Two nurses each want the same holiday off, and both care equally about having that particular day.
A colleague wants to change a unit protocol in a way the nurse believes conflicts with current evidence.
During a code, the charge nurse must quickly settle a disagreement between two nurses with no time to discuss it.
optionRationales: Correct. Accommodating works best when one person is much less invested in the issue than the other.
Incorrect. When both people are equally invested and a fair split is possible, compromising (such as alternating holidays) fits better than one person giving in.
Incorrect. A disagreement about evidence-based practice deserves collaboration, not self-sacrifice.
Incorrect. In an emergency with no time to talk, a quick directive (competing) decision protects the client; accommodating would waste critical time.
questions.rationale: Accommodating means satisfying others’ concerns while setting aside one’s own. It works best when one party is much less invested than the other—as with a break swap the nurse does not care about while a coworker urgently needs it. When both parties care equally, compromising fits better; in an emergency, a quick directive decision is needed. The protocol option is tempting because keeping peace with a colleague seems kind, but the issue matters to client outcomes and calls for collaborating.
questions.takeaway: Accommodate when you care much less than the other person—and never at the expense of safety.
questions.hintContent: Look for the situation in which the nurse has the least at stake.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate any option in which yielding would risk client safety; then apply the style’s best-use rule.
questions.ref: Module 37 · Collaboration · Conflict & Incivility · pp. 2559–2563

questions.stem: A client’s son approaches the nurses’ station and shouts, “My father has been waiting an hour for his pain medicine! Nobody here cares!” Which response by the nurse is most appropriate initially?
options: “Please lower your voice; other clients are trying to rest right now.”
“You’re worried about your father’s pain. Let’s go check on him together.”
“I understand you’re upset. Please have a seat while I check on him.”
“Let me look up when his last dose was given and what is ordered.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Correcting his behavior first ignores the fear behind it and is likely to escalate him.
Correct. Acknowledging the emotion and going to assess the father addresses both the son’s fear and the client’s pain, and involves the son.
Incorrect. Going to check on him is right, but “I understand” is a stock phrase, and sending the son to sit removes his sense of control instead of involving him.
Incorrect. Checking the record is needed, but it ignores the son’s emotion and delays going to the bedside to assess the father’s pain.
questions.rationale: Family anger often reflects fear and loss of control. The best initial response acknowledges the feeling, moves toward the client to assess and treat the pain, and involves the family—restoring some control and de-escalating tension. Asking him to lower his voice is the tempting distractor because the noise affects other clients, but leading with a correction communicates that the nurse cares more about the noise than his father. Sending the son to wait or starting with the chart leaves him out and delays the bedside assessment.
questions.takeaway: With an angry family, acknowledge the emotion, address the client’s need, and involve them.
questions.hintContent: Which response meets the son’s emotional need and the client’s physical need at once?
questions.hintStrategy: In therapeutic communication items, choose the response that reflects feelings and moves toward the client’s need.

questions.stem: A nurse educator is teaching staff to recognize incivility, horizontal violence, and bullying. Which behaviors should staff identify as examples? Select all that apply.
options: Rolling eyes and sighing whenever a new nurse asks a question
Repeatedly leaving key information out of one nurse’s handoff
Giving a peer private, specific feedback about a missed assessment
A group of nurses routinely excluding one peer from breaks
Asking a peer to repeat back a verbal order to check accuracy
Disagreeing respectfully with a colleague during a staff meeting
optionRationales: Correct. Eye-rolling and sighing are disrespectful, uncivil behaviors that discourage questions.
Correct. Repeatedly withholding needed information is sabotage, a form of workplace bullying that endangers clients.
Incorrect. Private, specific, respectful feedback aimed at improvement is constructive, not uncivil.
Correct. Peer exclusion by a group of equals is horizontal (lateral) violence.
Incorrect. Requesting a read-back is a standard closed-loop safety practice.
Incorrect. Respectful open disagreement is healthy overt conflict.
questions.rationale: Incivility is rude or disrespectful behavior; horizontal violence is hostility toward peers of equal standing; bullying is repeated, health-harming mistreatment that can include sabotage such as withholding information. All damage communication and client safety because targets stop asking questions and lose needed information. Constructive private feedback and respectful disagreement are tempting picks because they involve criticism or conflict, but they are professional behaviors that improve care.
questions.takeaway: Disrespect, exclusion, and sabotage are incivility or bullying; respectful feedback and disagreement are not.
questions.hintContent: Separate behaviors aimed at the person from behaviors aimed at improving care.
questions.hintStrategy: For behavior-classification SATA items, test each option against the definition’s key features (disrespect, repetition, harm).

questions.stem: A nurse manager notices growing tension among staff, who complain that “the same people always get the hardest assignments.” Which action by the manager is most likely to prevent further conflict?
options: Meet privately with each nurse who complained to hear their concerns in detail.
Set transparent criteria for distributing workload and invite staff feedback on them.
Rotate the charge nurse role each week so that no one person makes all assignments.
Publicly thank staff who accept the heaviest assignments at each staff meeting.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Listening is a good start, but private meetings do not change how assignments are made, so the perceived unfairness continues.
Correct. Allocating workloads fairly and inviting feedback without fear of punishment are leadership strategies for preventing conflict.
Incorrect. Rotating who decides does not fix the fairness of how assignments are made.
Incorrect. Acknowledging hard work is a leadership strategy, but praise does not make the workload any fairer and may reinforce the imbalance.
questions.rationale: Nursing leaders prevent conflict by allocating resources and workloads fairly, defining role expectations clearly, encouraging staff to raise concerns without fear of punitive action, and acknowledging accomplishments. Transparent workload criteria address the cause staff named and invite their input. Rotating charge nurses is tempting because it seems to share power, but without fair criteria the same perception of unfairness persists. Listening privately or praising hard workers helps morale but leaves the unfair system in place.
questions.takeaway: Leaders prevent conflict with fair, transparent workloads and nonpunitive feedback.
questions.hintContent: Which option fixes the actual cause the staff described?
questions.hintStrategy: For prevention items, choose the option that targets the root cause rather than the symptom.
questions.ref: Module 37 · Collaboration · Conflict & Incivility · pp. 2559–2563

questions.stem: The nurse educator reviews conflict management with new graduate nurses. Which statement by a new nurse indicates a need for further teaching?
options: “A unit with healthy teamwork has eliminated conflict completely.”
“Taking a short break to cool down can help before we talk it out.”
“Covert conflict can show up as tardiness and absenteeism on a unit.”
“When handled well, conflict can lead to better ways of giving care.”
optionRationales: Correct. Conflict is a normal, inevitable part of work that can be managed but never completely eliminated.
Incorrect. Temporary avoidance to regain composure can be effective.
Incorrect. Tardiness and absenteeism are repressive behaviors of covert conflict.
Incorrect. Constructively managed conflict can be an impetus for growth and safer care.
questions.rationale: Conflict is a normal and inevitable part of the work environment; it cannot be completely eliminated, but it can be managed constructively. A unit that appears conflict-free may actually be suppressing disagreement into covert forms. The other statements are accurate: brief avoidance can let emotions settle, covert conflict appears as tardiness and absenteeism, and well-managed conflict drives improvement.
questions.takeaway: Conflict is inevitable; the goal is constructive management, not elimination.
questions.hintContent: Find the statement that sets an impossible goal.
questions.hintStrategy: Absolute words such as “completely,” “always,” and “never” often mark the incorrect statement in teaching items.

questions.stem: Two nurses who disagreed about how to divide care for a client in isolation met with the charge nurse, who facilitated the discussion. Which statement by one of the nurses best indicates that the conflict was resolved through collaboration?
options: “I let her have her way this time, since it wasn’t worth an argument.”
“We each gave up something, so neither of us is completely happy.”
“We built a plan we both support and will check how it works Friday.”
“The charge nurse decided for us, so at least the argument is over.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Yielding to the other nurse is accommodating.
Incorrect. Partial satisfaction on both sides describes compromising.
Correct. A jointly built plan both support, with planned follow-up, reflects a win–win collaborative resolution.
Incorrect. A decision imposed by the charge nurse ends the dispute but is not collaborative and may leave resentment.
questions.rationale: Collaborative resolution produces a plan that both parties support because it meets both sets of concerns, and good conflict management includes follow-up to evaluate whether the plan works. Compromise is the closest distractor—it is a valid resolution style, but it leaves each nurse only partly satisfied. Accommodating and an imposed decision end the argument without true agreement, which increases the risk the conflict will return.
questions.takeaway: Collaboration ends with a shared plan both parties support—and a follow-up.
questions.hintContent: Which statement shows both nurses fully supporting the outcome?
questions.hintStrategy: In evaluation items, choose the statement that shows the stated goal—here, a win–win—was actually met.
questions.ref: Module 37 · Collaboration · Conflict & Incivility · pp. 2559–2563

questions.stem: A charge nurse is mediating a disagreement between an LPN and a UAP about who is responsible for a client’s hygiene care. Which actions by the charge nurse are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Meeting with both staff members in a private room
Letting each person explain without interruption
Asking, “How can we make sure his care gets done?”
Deciding who is right before hearing both sides
Reviewing each person’s past performance problems
optionRationales: Correct. Conflict should be discussed privately, away from client care areas.
Correct. Allowing each person to express concerns without interruption is a core guideline.
Correct. A team-centered “we” question focuses on solutions and client care.
Incorrect. Judging before hearing all viewpoints violates the guideline to hear everyone without passing judgment.
Incorrect. Bringing up past problems is destructive criticism and shifts focus from the current issue.
questions.rationale: Guidelines for managing conflict include discussing it privately, stating the issue objectively, hearing all viewpoints without judgment, letting each person speak without interruption, focusing on solutions, keeping client care central, and using team-centered “we” statements. Deciding early may feel efficient but skips the listening that makes a resolution stick. Raising past performance issues is destructive criticism that escalates conflict.
questions.takeaway: Mediate privately, listen to everyone without interrupting, and focus “we” on the client’s care.
questions.hintContent: Ask whether each action helps the parties feel heard and focuses on the client.
questions.hintStrategy: For process SATA items, reject options that judge, blame, or skip listening.
questions.ref: Module 37 · Collaboration · Conflict & Incivility · pp. 2559–2563

questions.stem: A new graduate nurse tells the charge nurse that her preceptor repeatedly criticizes her in front of clients and yesterday left a client’s fluid restriction out of report, which nearly caused an error. Which response by the charge nurse is most appropriate?
options: “Let’s complete a safety report about the missed fluid restriction.”
“I’ll talk with your preceptor today about how she gives report.”
“I can quietly find you a new preceptor so no one else needs to be involved.”
“Let’s document these incidents and report them to the nurse manager.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. A safety report for the near miss is appropriate, but it addresses only one event and not the pattern of bullying behavior.
Incorrect. Addressing the preceptor is reasonable, but an informal talk without documentation or the manager is unlikely to stop a repeated pattern that affects safety.
Incorrect. Quietly reassigning avoids the behavior and leaves the near miss and the preceptor’s conduct unaddressed.
Correct. Documenting specific incidents and reporting through the chain of command per policy addresses the bullying and the safety risk.
questions.rationale: Repeated public criticism and withholding report information are workplace bullying—repeated, harmful mistreatment that includes sabotage—and the near miss shows client safety is affected. The appropriate response is to document specific incidents and report them to the nurse manager according to policy, along with a safety report for the near miss. Quietly finding a new preceptor is tempting because it protects the new nurse quickly, but it is avoidance: the behavior continues for the next orientee, and the system issue is never addressed.
questions.takeaway: Bullying that affects client safety must be documented and reported through the chain of command.
questions.hintContent: The behavior is repeated and has already affected a client—what does that require?
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate responses that normalize, publicize, or quietly avoid; choose the one that uses the proper channel.
questions.ref: Module 37 · Collaboration · Conflict & Incivility · pp. 2559–2563
